Ren, T., Patel, M. and Blok, K. (2006). Olefins from conventional and heavy feedstocks: Energy use in steam cracking and alternative processes. Energy 31, 425-451. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.energy.2005.04.001

Loaded: specific energy consumption (per t ethylene and per t HVC, primary-energy basis) and CO2 intensity of typical ethane and naphtha steam crackers (Table 2), propane cracking (Table 5 note c), the paper's aggregate for state-of-the-art naphtha cracking (Section 6.1), and total energy use and status of six alternative olefin routes (Table 5); average cracker capacity; derived feed/hydrogen/methane flows per t HVC from Table 2 yields. Not loaded: per-licensor SECs of Table 4 (reprinted claims; other-values), yields, temperatures, section shares and exergy losses (other-values), savings of advanced cracking technologies and byproduct upgrading (measures sidecar), global totals. No costs are given in the paper.

(1) All energy figures are primary energy (electricity at 40%, steam at 85%) whereas the database SEC is final energy; for crackers the gap is small (electricity approx. 1 GJ/t ethylene primary, steam internal) but alternative routes include primary energy of imported oxygen, hydrogen and steam. (2) Most Table 2 and Table 4 values are reprinted from other sources ([19,21,22]) and rounded as "approximately". (3) Table 5 prints single figures for "GJ/t ethylene/HVCs" for gas-feed routes. (4) CPP reaction temperature is 600-700 degC in Table 5 but 650-750 degC in the text (p.444); catalytic naphtha SEC is approx. 10 GJ/t HVCs in Table 5 but 10-11 in the text (p.441). (5) Two CO2 figures for typical naphtha cracking: 1.8-2.0 t/t ethylene in Table 2 but "average 1.6 t/t ethylene in Table 2" in footnote 10 (1.6 is the per-HVC value). (6) HVC definition weights non-olefins at 50%, differing from EC-BREF, so per-HVC SECs are not directly comparable with other sources.
